subject: 🥊 Tougher Fed battle
body_html:
Plus: Super-low jobless claims | Thursday, November 12, 2026
 
View in browser
 
 
Axios Macro
By Neil Irwin and Courtenay Brown · Nov 12, 2026

The bond market is once again flashing a warning sign as hard-to-beat inflation raises the odds of a longer, more aggressive tightening campaign.

  • More below. Plus, new data points to remarkably low layoffs across the U.S. economy.

Today's newsletter, edited by Jeffrey Cane and copy edited by Katie Lewis, is 887 words, a 3.5-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: Fed's inflation reckoning
 
Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

Inflation is no longer confined to a handful of trouble spots. Now, Federal Reserve officials are starting to question whether raising interest rates gradually will be enough to contain it.

Why it matters: Fed officials had hoped that a relatively modest series of interest rate hikes would be enough to bring inflation under control — more a recalibration than a tightening campaign.

  • But stubbornly high — and increasingly widespread — price pressures are raising the possibility of a more prolonged tightening campaign, with no clear endpoint in sight.
  • That would leave the Fed facing a more difficult balancing act: raising rates enough to contain inflation without unnecessarily damaging the economy.

What they're saying: "We have got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing — and we're going to have to deal with that," Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee, who called the inflation data "borderline disturbing," said late Tuesday.

Driving the news: Treasury yields are surging after Tuesday's hot inflation report and hawkish commentary from Fed officials — including governor Christopher Waller, who raised the prospect of a supersized rate hike next month.

  • Short-term yields have risen more sharply than longer-term yields, a sign that investors expect the Fed may need to raise rates more aggressively than previously anticipated.
  • The yield on the two-year Treasury note is still marching higher after surging 17 basis points on Tuesday, which was the biggest one-day surge since April 2025 — when markets were reeling from the "liberation day" tariffs.
  • The yield on the 10-year Treasury note jumped about 8 basis points, putting it back above 5%.
  • Financial markets see a December rate hike as virtually certain, according to CME FedWatch. Expectations for next year are trending higher, with traders now pricing in two additional quarter-point hikes by June.

The big picture: Measures designed to strip out unusually large price swings suggest that underlying inflation pressures are gaining pace.

  • The Cleveland Fed's trimmed-mean Consumer Price Index —which filters out unusually large price swings to give a clearer picture of underlying inflation — rose 0.4% in October, the largest monthly increase since May.
  • The Atlanta Fed's sticky-price CPI, which tracks prices that typically change, slowly accelerated to a 4.7% annualized pace in October, its fastest since February 2025.
  • More than three-quarters of the consumer price basket saw prices rise at an annualized rate exceeding 2% in October, the largest share since August 2022, Charles Schwab's head of macro research Kevin Gordon posted on X.

Yes, but: The Fed may have reason to proceed cautiously even against the backdrop of stubborn inflation.

  • Rising bond yields and a sell-off in technology stocks (revived again by the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang) are already tightening financial conditions — potentially doing some of the work of higher interest rates.
  • Fed governor Michelle Bowman said in a speech that falling stock prices, higher borrowing costs and a stronger dollar could weigh on economic growth, particularly in sectors already struggling with high interest rates.
  • Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who dissented against the decision to hold rates steady last month, said she still supported a more gradual approach to raising rates. "It's less disruptive to the overall economy than moving in sharper, more aggressive movements," she said this morning.

What to watch: Some of the forces driving inflation higher this year — including tariffs and the Iran war — were expected to be temporary. But the risk that they will prove more persistent keeps resurfacing.

  • President Trump threatened this morning to double tariffs on Mexican imports unless the nation stops a caravan of migrants from reaching the U.S. border.
  • Trump also said the U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran, raising fresh questions about how soon the conflict (and the disruption to global energy supplies) might end.

2. Low, low layoffs
 
Data: Labor Department; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

The pace of layoffs has been historically low — and the latest data on weekly jobless claims points to the pattern continuing.

Driving the news: Only 200,000 people filed new claims for unemployment benefits last week.

  • That was the ninth consecutive week of claims being at or below 200,000, the first time that has happened in a data series that dates to 1967.
  • The four-week moving average of claims was stable at 195,250 for the second consecutive week, an all-time low.
  • The number of continuing claims for unemployment benefits was 1.697 million last week, near three-year lows. (It was slightly lower, 1.695 million, for one week last month.)

State of play: The recent claims data aligns with other evidence that, even as employers are not going gangbusters in hiring new staff, they are unusually reluctant to cut current workers from their payrolls.

  • For example, the rate of layoffs and discharges was 1% in September, only a tick above the all-time low of 0.9% reached in the ultra-hot job market of 2021.
  • Fed officials have pointed to the low jobless claims as evidence of a relatively strong job market — one that allows them to focus their attention on inflation.

The bottom line: The economy has plenty of problems, but mass layoffs aren't among them.
